audience: For founders and people responsible for an AI product
h1: Does AI regulation reach your business?
sub: Five questions, in plain words. No account, nothing to install, and nothing you type here leaves your browser. At the end you get a list of what your answers point at and what a person still has to settle.
meta: Regula indicates where to look. It does not decide your risk tier, your obligations, or whether you comply. This is not legal advice.

home.eyebrow: Local code observation and evidence preparation
home.title: Know what your code can show. Know what still needs judgement.
home.lead: Regula connects declared deployment facts with code-observable indicators, then shows the questions a person still needs to resolve. It is a review path, not an automated compliance verdict.

home.journeysEyebrow: Start with the task in front of you
home.journeysLead: Choose the route that matches your responsibility. Each path says what the tool can produce and where human judgement begins.

journeys.body: Record where the system is used, what it does and which operator role may apply.
Run the local CLI, review matched indicators and keep proprietary source on your machine.
Keep declared facts, observations, unresolved questions and evidence scaffolds separate.
Inspect coverage levels, methods, benchmark limits, security and accessibility evidence.

questions.legend: Do you sell to, or have users in, the EU?
questions.help: The rules can reach a business based anywhere. What matters is whether your product, or what your product produces, is used by people in the EU.

questions.legend: Does your product use AI at all?
questions.help: This includes AI you did not build: a chatbot, a model you call through someone else's service, or a feature a no-code tool added for you.

questions.legend: Did you build the AI, or are you using someone else's?
questions.help: Operator role is one fact a reviewer must establish. Building, placing on the market and using a system can point to different provisions, and one organisation can hold more than one role.

questions.legend: Do people see content your AI produced, or talk to it directly?
questions.help: Text, images, audio, video, or a chatbot can make Article 50 worth reviewing. The actor, purpose, paragraph, conditions and exceptions still matter.

questions.legend: Does AI help decide something about a person?
questions.help: Hiring, credit, insurance, education, healthcare or benefits can make Annex III worth reviewing. Intended purpose and the Article 6 conditions and exceptions still need evidence.

errorOne: One question is still unanswered. It is highlighted below, and “Not sure” is a real answer if you do not know.
errorMany: {n} questions are still unanswered. They are highlighted below, and “Not sure” is a real answer if you do not know.
clearedNotice: Your answers have been cleared. The five questions are ready again.
ledeIn: Below is what your own answers point at, and what they cannot settle. None of it is a decision about your risk tier or your obligations, because those depend on facts that five questions cannot reach.
ledeNoEu: Nothing you have told us connects you to the EU market, so the EU AI Act may not be the first thing to look at. That is a scoping question rather than a conclusion, and what follows says why it is not settled.
ledeNoAi: You have said your product does not use AI. The Act works from its own definition, which is broader than most people expect, so this is worth checking rather than assuming.
pointsHeading: Worth reading, based on what you said
humanDecisionEmpty: Not recorded. This field stays empty until an accountable reviewer interprets the evidence.

scope.title: An Article 2 scope connection to review
scope.body: You said people in the EU use your product. Article 2 is potentially relevant, including its conditions for providers and deployers established in a third country. A reviewer still needs to confirm the operator, territorial facts and exclusions.
scope.linkText: Does the EU AI Act apply to your app?

scopeUnsure.title: Whether the rules reach you is the first thing to settle
scopeUnsure.body: You are not sure whether people in the EU use your product. That is the first question to answer, because Article 2 covers providers and deployers established in a third country where the output produced by the AI system is used in the Union. It turns on where your users are and where your output ends up.
scopeUnsure.linkText: Does the EU AI Act apply to your app?

noEu.title: Nothing you told us connects you to the EU market
noEu.body: You said your product is not sold to, and not used by, people in the EU. Article 2 can still reach an organisation established in a third country where the output produced by the AI system is used in the Union, so it is worth knowing where your output ends up. Other countries are legislating too, and this site tracks several of them.

noAi.title: The definition is broader than most people expect
noAi.body: You said your product does not use AI. The Act works from its own definition in Article 3(1), which turns on what a system does with the input it receives rather than on which technology built it. If anything in your product infers, predicts, recommends or generates, check it against the definition rather than assume.

definition.title: Whether it is an AI system in the Act's own sense
definition.body: This is the first thing a person has to settle, and five plain questions cannot settle it. Article 3(1) turns on what the system does with the input it receives, not on the product label, the library it imports, or whether anyone calls it AI.

roleProvider.title: The provider-role question to review
roleProvider.body: You said you built or trained the system. Article 3(3) may be relevant, but engineering authorship does not establish the legal role. A reviewer must confirm how the system is placed on the market or put into service and under whose name.

roleDeployer.title: The deployer-role question to review
roleDeployer.body: You said you use someone else's system. Article 3(4) may be relevant, but this answer alone does not establish your role or duties. A reviewer must confirm whose authority governs the use and how the product reaches people.

roleBoth.title: More than one operator role may need review
roleBoth.body: You said both. Articles 3(3), 3(4) and 25(1) are potentially relevant to a review of roles, branding, modifications and intended purpose. The answer does not establish that either role or any attached duty applies.

roleUnsure.title: Your role is one of the facts to settle first
roleUnsure.body: You are not sure. Articles 3(3), 3(4) and 25(1) distinguish roles using facts about market placement, authority, branding, modifications and intended purpose. Preserve the uncertainty and ask a reviewer to establish the role from evidence.

transparency.title: Article 50 context to review
transparency.body: You said people see AI-produced content or talk to the system directly. That is a code and context indicator, not an applicability decision. A reviewer must identify the actor, purpose, relevant paragraph, conditions and exceptions before deciding whether any disclosure or marking duty applies.

decisions.title: Annex III and Article 6 context to review
decisions.body: You said AI helps decide something about a person. Annex III and Article 6 may be relevant, but this answer does not determine a legal tier. A reviewer must confirm intended purpose, the listed use, the Article 6(3) conditions, profiling and any exceptions from evidence.

prohibited.title: Article 5 practices still require a separate review
prohibited.body: This short questionnaire did not collect the purpose, target, safeguards, conditions and exceptions needed to review Article 5. Read the listed practices and preserve unresolved facts rather than infer either prohibition or safety.

unsettled: Whether what you have meets the Act's own definition of an AI system. Article 3(1) is the test, and it is not the same as whether you call it AI.
Which role or roles you occupy. That depends on how the system reaches the people who use it, not on who wrote the code.
Your intended purpose. Most classification turns on it, and it is a statement you make rather than something a tool can read.
Whether any of the Article 6(3) conditions applies to you, and whether anything you do removes it.
Everything that lives in your contracts, your governance and how the system behaves once it is running. No scanner can see any of it, and neither can five questions.

free.title: Keep going, free
free.body: Work through the fuller assessment in your browser. It asks the same ground in the law's own terms and shows where each question comes from. No account, and nothing you enter is uploaded. If you use the terminal command below, replace COMMIT_SHA with the full public commit hash you reviewed. The scanner runs on your own machine and does not upload your code.
free.short: Free, in your browser or your terminal. No account, nothing uploaded.

paid.title: Use the local CLI
paid.body: Run the same code-observable indicators on your own machine. The CLI produces text and stable JSON output, unresolved facts, and evidence scaffolds without uploading scanned files. Its output is an input to review, not a compliance determination, certification or legal opinion.
paid.short: Local code observations and evidence scaffolds. Free and open source.

consultant.title: Get independent review
consultant.body: Regula does not operate a paid review, booking service, certification or law practice. When intended purpose, operator role, deployment context or legal interpretation changes the answer, take the relevant evidence to an appropriately qualified professional you select independently.
consultant.short: Human judgment for context Regula cannot observe. Not provided by Regula.

consultantWarranted: Your answers raise context that warrants careful human review. Another automated signal cannot settle intended purpose, operator role, conditions or exceptions.
limits: Regula indicates where to look. It does not decide your risk tier, your obligations, or whether you comply. Conformity is determined by regulators and notified bodies, not by a questionnaire, and “not flagged” never means “compliant”.
Nothing here is legal advice. Anything that turns on a legal conclusion needs an appropriately qualified professional.
